source.nom: Raichle & Gusnard, PNAS, 2002 (budget énergétique du cerveau)

rappel.q: How many watts does the brain produce?

cards.titre: Your brain generates enough energy to light a light bulb
cards.texte: The human brain produces about 20 watts during normal activity. That's as much as a standard LED light bulb. It never shuts off while you sleep.
cards.action: Try it today: place your hand on your forehead and think: "20 watts are running here, even at night."

source.nom: Smithsonian Ocean, fiche Octopus

rappel.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?

cards.titre: Octopuses have 3 hearts and blue blood
cards.texte: Their blood contains hemocyanin, which is copper-based, instead of iron-based hemoglobin: it is blue. Their main heart stops when they swim, which is why they often prefer to crawl along the bottom.
cards.action: Try this today: draw an octopus with its 3 hearts.

source.nom: Smithsonian Ocean, Sharks & Rays ; Wikipédia, Archaeopteris

rappel.q: Who appeared first?

cards.titre: Sharks existed before trees
cards.texte: The first sharks appeared about 450 million years ago. The first true trees appeared about 60 to 90 million years later. Sharks have survived 5 mass extinctions.
cards.action: Try it today: tell someone this fact and ask them to guess who appeared first.

source.nom: Calcul : 0,1 mm × 2⁴² ≈ 440 000 km ; distance Terre-Lune ≈ 384 000 km (NASA)

rappel.q: What does the thickness do at each fold?

cards.titre: Folding a sheet of paper 42 times exceeds the Moon
cards.texte: The thickness doubles with each fold. After 42 folds: 440,000 km. The Moon is 384,000 km away. At fold 103, the sheet would have the diameter of the observable Universe.
cards.action: Try it today: try folding a sheet of paper in half as many times as possible: you will rarely exceed 7.

source.nom: Thermodynamique de base ; zéro absolu = −273,15 °C (BIPM)

rappel.q: What is cold?

cards.titre: Cold does not physically exist
cards.texte: "Cold" is the absence of heat, just as darkness is the absence of light. You can't "send cold"—you remove heat. Absolute zero (-273°C) is the limit.
cards.action: Try it today: touch a metal spoon: feel the warmth of your hand transfer into it.

source.nom: Wikipédia, Effet Mpemba

rappel.q: What is this effect called?

cards.titre: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water
cards.texte: This is the Mpemba effect: in some experiments, hot water freezes before cold water. Scientists are still debating when and why it occurs: container, evaporation, dissolved gases…
cards.action: Try it today: ask an adult if they know about the Mpemba effect.

source.nom: CNRTL, étymologie de « bonjour »

rappel.q: From which words does "hello" come?

cards.titre: "Hello" was initially a wish
cards.texte: "Bonjour" comes from "bon jour": it was a way of wishing someone a good day. In the Middle Ages, people also said "Dieu vous donne bon jour" (God give you a good day). The expression has been used for over 700 years.
cards.action: Try it today: say "hello" to 3 people while thinking about its true meaning.

source.nom: USGS, The Water in You

rappel.q: What part of the body is water?

cards.titre: You are 60% water… which existed before the dinosaurs.
cards.texte: Your body is made up of about 60% water. The hydrogen atoms in this water formed shortly after the Big Bang, nearly 14 billion years ago. The water you drink has already circled the planet thousands of times.
cards.action: Try it today: while drinking a glass of water, imagine all the trips she has taken.

source.nom: Giraud et al., PNAS, 2002

rappel.q: Where does this supercolony extend?

cards.titre: Argentine ants form a colony spanning 6,000 km²
cards.texte: A supercolony of Argentine ants extends over approximately 6,000 km along the Mediterranean coast. Ants from very distant places do not attack each other: they recognize each other as one large family.
cards.action: Try this today: observe ants outside: do they all follow the same path?

source.nom: Rupa Marya v. Warner/Chappell (2015), règlement en 2016

rappel.q: What happened in 2016?

cards.titre: "Happy Birthday" was copyrighted until 2016
cards.texte: A company was earning approximately $2 million a year from this song. A lawsuit showed that its rights were invalid, and the song has been free since 2016. Its melody comes from a children's song published in 1893.
cards.action: Try it today: sing "Happy Birthday": you have the right, she is free!

source.nom: NASA, mesures laser Apollo (Lunar Laser Ranging)

rappel.q: How far does the Moon move away from Earth each year?

cards.titre: The Moon moves 3.8 cm away from the Earth each year
cards.texte: In 600 million years, it will be too far away to cover the Sun during total eclipses. The perfect eclipses we see are a temporary cosmic anomaly.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, look at the Moon and think that it is moving away just a little bit.

source.nom: Smithsonian, Butterflies taste with their feet

rappel.q: What does the butterfly taste?

cards.titre: Butterflies taste with their legs
cards.texte: Butterflies have taste receptors on their legs. When they land on a plant, they immediately know if it is suitable for laying their eggs.
cards.action: Try it today: taste a food with your eyes closed and guess what it is.

source.nom: Spalding, Frisén et al., Cell, 2005

rappel.q: Which cells often last a lifetime?

cards.titre: Your body constantly renews a large part of its cells
cards.texte: Skin, blood, and intestines renew themselves in a few days or weeks. But some cells, like many neurons or those in the lens of the eye, can last a lifetime. The idea that "everything is replaced in 7 years" is a myth.
cards.action: Try it today: look at a picture of yourself as a baby: many of your cells have changed since then.

source.nom: NASA, Lightning Climatology

rappel.q: How many lightning strikes occur per second on Earth?

cards.titre: Lightning strikes the Earth approximately 44 times per second
cards.texte: That's more than 3 million lightning strikes per day on the planet. A single lightning strike can heat the air to nearly 30,000°C, about 5 times the temperature of the Sun's surface.
cards.action: Try it today: at the next thunderstorm, count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder.

source.nom: Simard et al., Nature, 1997 ; Karst et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023

rappel.q: What would the roots be connected to?

cards.titre: Trees communicate underground via fungi
cards.texte: The roots of many trees are connected to fungi that exchange water and nutrients. Some researchers believe that trees help each other in this way, but the extent of this "Wood Wide Web" is still debated.
cards.action: Try this today: in the forest or park, look for mushrooms at the base of the trees.

source.nom: NASA Science, Venus Facts

rappel.q: What is longer on Venus?

cards.titre: On Venus, a day lasts longer than a year.
cards.texte: Venus rotates very slowly on its axis: about 243 Earth days for one rotation. But it orbits the Sun in 225 days. Its year is therefore shorter than its day!
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, look for Venus: it is often the brightest point after sunset.

source.nom: Futura Sciences, Pourquoi la tour Eiffel change-t-elle de taille ? (2023)

rappel.q: Why does the Eiffel Tower grow taller in the summer?

cards.titre: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer
cards.texte: Iron expands when it is hot. During periods of intense heat, the tower can rise by about fifteen centimeters, and its top leans slightly to the side opposite the Sun.
cards.action: Try this today: observe a bridge: do you see any joints that allow the metal to move?

source.nom: Dyer, Neumeyer & Chittka, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2005

rappel.q: What did the bees learn from the experience?

cards.titre: Bees can recognize faces
cards.texte: In an experiment, bees learned to recognize a photo of a human face to obtain sugar water. Their brains are tiny, but very clever!
cards.action: Try this today: draw 3 different faces and ask someone to identify them.

source.nom: NASA, Moon Facts ; Geoscience Australia

rappel.q: Which is the widest?

cards.titre: Australia is wider than the Moon
cards.texte: The Moon is approximately 3,474 km in diameter. Australia is approximately 4,000 km from east to west. A country wider than an entire celestial body!
cards.action: Try it today: look at a map and find Australia.

source.nom: NASA, Can you hear sound in space?

rappel.q: Why is there no sound in space?

cards.titre: In space, no one can hear you scream.
cards.texte: Sound needs air or water to travel. In space, there is almost nothing: sounds do not pass through. Astronauts communicate by radio.
cards.action: Try it today: put your ear to a table and tap: sound also travels through objects.

source.nom: Henneberg, Lambert & Leigh, Nature, 1996

rappel.q: What animal has footprints like ours?

cards.titre: Koalas have fingerprints just like us
cards.texte: Koalas' fingerprints look so much like ours that it's difficult to tell the difference under a microscope. Yet, our ancestors are very distant.
cards.action: Try it today: press your finger on a window and look at your fingerprint.

source.nom: Loftus & Palmer, 1974 ; Nader et al., Nature, 2000

rappel.q: What does the brain do with each reminder?

cards.titre: Your brain reinvents your memories every time
cards.texte: Memory is not a recording. Each recall reconstructs the memory and alters it slightly. This is why two witnesses recount the same scene differently.
cards.action: Try it today: tell a memory with a loved one, then compare your versions.

source.nom: Coles et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2022 (Many Smiles Collaboration)

rappel.q: What do some studies suggest?

cards.titre: Smiling might slightly improve your mood
cards.texte: According to the "facial feedback" hypothesis, facial muscles send signals to the brain. Some studies suggest that a smile, even a voluntary one, slightly improves mood. The effect exists but is small, and researchers are still debating it.
cards.action: Try this today: smile for 10 seconds in front of a mirror and note if your mood changes.

source.nom: Diekelmann & Born, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2010

rappel.q: When does the brain consolidate memories?

cards.titre: Your brain consolidates your learning during sleep
cards.texte: At night, the hippocampus "replays" what you learned during the day and helps to store it in long-term memory. Sleeping after learning helps you remember it better.
cards.action: Try it today: reread your lesson before going to sleep, then recite it again when you wake up.

source.nom: Kruger & Dunning, JPSP, 1999

rappel.q: Who overestimates their abilities the most?

cards.titre: The Dunning-Kruger effect: novices think they're experts
cards.texte: People with limited expertise in a field tend to overestimate their abilities—because they lack the tools to measure their own ignorance. True experts are more self-doubting.
cards.action: Try it today: choose a subject where you believe you are strong and look for what you don't yet know.

source.nom: Vohs et al., JPSP, 2008 ; Hagger et al., 2016 (réplication discutée)

rappel.q: What are "small decisions" for the brain?

cards.titre: Making a decision tires your brain
cards.texte: Making too many choices in quick succession can lead to a feeling of fatigue, and some researchers refer to this as "decision fatigue." The effect is debated, but reducing the number of small decisions (such as preparing your belongings the night before) frees up your mind for what truly matters.
cards.action: Try it today: prepare your clothes for tomorrow tonight.

source.nom: Mark, Gudith & Klocke, CHI, 2008

rappel.q: How long does it take to return to a task?

cards.titre: After a break, it takes time to refocus.
cards.texte: A study by Gloria Mark (University of California) observed that it takes an average of 23 minutes to fully return to an interrupted task. Checking your phone every 10 minutes prevents you from achieving deep concentration.
cards.action: Try this today: put your phone in another room for 25 minutes while you work.

source.nom: Csikszentmihalyi, Flow, 1990 ; Dietrich, 2004 (hypothèse d’hypofrontalité)

rappel.q: What do we think about less during flow?

cards.titre: The "flow": when you forget about time
cards.texte: Flow is a state of total absorption in an activity. According to one hypothesis, the activity of certain areas of the prefrontal cortex, linked to self-criticism, decreases during this time: one thinks less about oneself and feels more efficient.
cards.action: Try it today: do an activity you enjoy for 20 minutes without any interruptions.

source.nom: Jecker & Landy, Human Relations, 1969

rappel.q: What do we often appreciate after helping someone?

cards.titre: Doing someone a favor makes them more favorable towards you
cards.texte: The Benjamin Franklin effect: when we do someone a favor, we tend to like them more afterwards. Our brain says: "If I helped them, it's because I like them."
cards.action: Try it today: ask a small favor of someone you don't know very well.

source.nom: Wieth & Zacks, Thinking & Reasoning, 2011

rappel.q: When do we find more original ideas?

cards.titre: Original ideas sometimes come when we're less alert.
cards.texte: A study has shown that we solve certain intuition problems better at our "non-optimal" time of day (evening for early risers). The brain filters less, and unexpected associations appear.
cards.action: Try this today: write down a weird idea that comes to you when you're a little tired.

source.nom: Jeannerod, NeuroImage, 2001 (imagerie motrice)

rappel.q: What does the brain do when we imagine an action?

cards.titre: Imagining a movement activates some of the same areas as doing it
cards.texte: Visualizing a sporting movement partially activates the motor areas used to perform it. This is why athletes also train mentally. But visualizing doesn't replace practice: it complements it.
cards.action: Try this today: before performing a sporting action, imagine it in detail 3 times.

source.nom: Roediger & Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006

rappel.q: What helps us remember better?

cards.titre: Testing oneself beats rereading
cards.texte: Students who practiced recalling a text retained significantly more a week later than those who reread it, even if they felt less confident at the time.
cards.action: Try it today: hide your lesson and write down everything you remember.

source.nom: Zajonc, JPSP, 1968

rappel.q: Why do ads repeat themselves?
choix: We like what we see again

cards.titre: We like what we see often
cards.texte: The more we see something, the more we tend to like it, even without realizing it. This is the mere-exposure effect, and that's why ads repeat themselves.
cards.action: Try it today: find a song that you like now but not the first time.

source.nom: Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans, Journal of Experimental Psychology: HPP, 2001

rappel.q: What does the brain do when "multitasking"?
choix: He moves from one task to another
He does everything at the same time

cards.titre: The brain doesn't really do two things at once.
cards.texte: When we think we are doing several things at the same time, the brain actually switches very quickly from one to the other. Each change costs time and results in errors.
cards.action: Try it today: do your homework for 20 minutes without any other activity.

source.nom: Delgado et al., Educational Research Review, 2018

rappel.q: What medium allows for better understanding?

cards.titre: We often understand a text better when it's on paper.
cards.texte: A large analysis of 54 studies shows that informational texts read on paper are somewhat better understood than those read on screen, especially when in a hurry.
cards.action: Try it today: read your next important lesson on paper.

source.nom: Oyserman, identité et motivation (identity-based motivation), 2009

rappel.q: What helps to maintain a habit?

cards.titre: Seeing yourself as "someone who does it" helps you to persevere
cards.texte: Instead of thinking "I'm trying to read more," think "I am a reader." Psychologists observe that we maintain a behavior better when it aligns with our self-image. Every small action reinforces this image.
cards.action: Try it today: choose one small action that resembles the person you want to become.

source.nom: Amabile & Kramer, The Progress Principle, 2011

rappel.q: What motivates you the most on a daily basis?
choix: To feel that one is making progress

cards.titre: Small victories create a chain of momentum
cards.texte: Feeling that you are making progress, even a little, makes you want to continue. Researchers have analyzed thousands of logbooks: the best days were those where progress was made on work that mattered.
cards.action: Try it today: complete a very small task and write it down.

source.nom: Bjork, « difficultés désirables », 1994

rappel.q: What often signals discomfort in learning?

cards.titre: The discomfort of learning is not a danger
cards.texte: Learning something difficult often feels unpleasant. Researchers refer to this as "desirable difficulty": an effort that costs a little actually helps with better retention.
cards.action: Try it today: do 5 minutes of something difficult that you keep putting off.

source.nom: David Allen, Getting Things Done, 2001 (règle des 2 minutes) ; Zeigarnik, 1927

rappel.q: What to do with a task that takes less than 2 minutes?
choix: Make a note of it for tomorrow

cards.titre: The 2-minute rule: if it takes less than 2 minutes, do it now
cards.texte: If a task takes less than 2 minutes, do it now. Unfinished tasks tend to linger in the back of your mind (Zeigarnik effect). Completing them frees your mind.
cards.action: Try this today: do 3 things right now that take less than 2 minutes.

source.nom: Locke & Latham, American Psychologist, 2002 ; Matthews, Dominican University, 2015

rappel.q: What helps to achieve a goal?

cards.titre: Writing down your goals helps you achieve them
cards.texte: Clear, written goals are more often achieved than vague intentions: this is one of the strongest findings in goal psychology. Writing things down forces you to clarify what you truly want.
cards.action: Try this today: write a specific goal on a piece of paper and display it.

source.nom: Duckworth et al., JPSP, 2007 ; Credé et al., 2017 (méta-analyse)

rappel.q: What does Angela Duckworth call this quality?

cards.titre: Perseverance counts, not just talent.
cards.texte: Angela Duckworth studied students, military cadets, and competition competitors. Long-term tenacity, which she calls "grit," helps with success. Other studies show that its effect is real but more modest than often claimed.
cards.action: Try it today: choose one thing you want to continue even when it's boring.

source.nom: Lally et al., European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010

rappel.q: How many days on average does it take for a habit to form?

cards.titre: A habit is formed in 66 days, not 21
cards.texte: The myth of "21 days" comes from a misreading of a book from the 1960s. A 2010 study found an average of 66 days, with variations from 18 to 254 days depending on the person and habit.
cards.action: Try it today: choose a habit and tick off each day you do it.

source.nom: Gollwitzer, intentions de mise en œuvre, 1999

rappel.q: What should you do upon waking, according to this map?

cards.titre: Choose your priority for the day first thing in the morning
cards.texte: There's no magic in the first five minutes, but deciding early on what matters helps you stick to it. Starting with a clear intention rather than notifications prevents others from deciding your day.
cards.action: Try it today: when you wake up, choose just one thing that is important for your day.

source.nom: Deci & Ryan, théorie de l’autodétermination, 1985 ; Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999

rappel.q: Which motivation lasts the longest?

cards.titre: Inner pride is a greater motivator than external reward.
cards.texte: Research on motivation shows that doing something because you find it interesting or important lasts longer than doing it solely for an external reward.
cards.action: Try it today: do one thing just for the pleasure of succeeding at it.

source.nom: Dweck, Mindset, 2006 ; Yeager et al., Nature, 2019

rappel.q: Who has studied the growth mindset?

cards.titre: Believing that you can improve helps you learn from your mistakes
cards.texte: Carol Dweck (Stanford) has shown that believing one's abilities can be developed helps one bounce back after failure. Large studies find modest effects on average, but more pronounced effects among struggling students.
cards.action: Try it today: when you fail, ask yourself, "What am I learning?"

source.nom: Driskell, Copper & Moran, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1994 (méta-analyse)

rappel.q: Who uses visualization a lot?

cards.titre: Practicing in your mind really helps
cards.texte: To accurately imagine an active performance, partially using the same areas as the actual action. A meta-analysis shows that mental training improves performance, especially when combined with real-world practice.
cards.action: Try this today: visualize a difficult exercise from beginning to end before doing it.

source.nom: Principe d’activation comportementale (Jacobson et al., 1996)

rappel.q: What often comes first?

cards.titre: Action comes before motivation, not the other way around.
cards.texte: We often wait until we're motivated to act, but it's often the other way around: starting makes you want to continue. Just give it a try for two minutes; the momentum comes from doing.
cards.action: Try it today: start a task in just 2 minutes, without waiting until you feel like it.

source.nom: Csikszentmihalyi, Flow, 1990

rappel.q: What happens when a challenge is too easy?

cards.titre: The brain is designed for challenges of the right difficulty
cards.texte: The flow state (Csikszentmihalyi) occurs when the challenge slightly exceeds your capabilities. Too easy = boredom. Too difficult = anxiety. The sweet spot = maximum growth.
cards.action: Try this today: make an exercise a little harder than usual, not by much.

source.nom: Wagner et al., Nature, 2004 (sommeil et intuition)

rappel.q: What does the brain do with a problem at night?
choix: He continues to work on it

cards.titre: Sleeping on a problem isn't laziness — it's strategy
cards.texte: In one experiment, people who slept after an exercise were twice as likely to discover a hidden trick as those who stayed awake. Sleep helps the brain reorganize what it has learned.
cards.action: Try this today: reread a difficult problem before going to sleep, without looking for the solution.

source.nom: Harkin et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2016

rappel.q: What helps to stick to a goal?

cards.titre: Having a chat with someone helps you stick to your goals
cards.texte: A large meta-analysis shows that tracking progress helps achieve goals, especially when it's recorded or shared. Scheduling a follow-up appointment with someone makes the commitment more tangible.
cards.action: Try it today: tell a close friend or family member your goal and set a time to talk about it again.

source.nom: Terry et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2020 (méta-analyse)

rappel.q: What does music reduce during exercise?

cards.titre: Rhythmic music helps during exertion
cards.texte: A meta-analysis on music and sport shows that it reduces the perception of effort, improves mood, and slightly enhances performance. Rhythms of approximately 120 to 140 beats per minute are often used.
cards.action: Try it today: do 10 minutes of exercise to rhythmic music.

source.nom: Harkin et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2016

rappel.q: What helps one progress?

cards.titre: Tracking your progress helps you improve
cards.texte: A meta-analysis of over 130 studies shows that monitoring progress helps achieve goals. Seeing progress creates a positive feedback loop. Even a simple chart with crosses is enough.
cards.action: Try it today: draw a chart and tick off one successful habit each day.

source.nom: Wood & Neal, habitudes et contexte ; Wood, Good Habits, Bad Habits, 2019

rappel.q: What helps more than willpower?

cards.titre: The environment matters more than willpower
cards.texte: Instead of fighting your cravings, change your space: put the fruit where you can see it and put the cakes away. Research on habits shows that the environment guides many of our automatic choices.
cards.action: Try it today: tidy up your space so that the good habit is as easy as possible.

source.nom: Nietzsche, Crépuscule des idoles (1889) ; Yeager et al., JPSP, 2014

rappel.q: What helps one to persevere?

cards.titre: Knowing why you do things helps you persevere
cards.texte: Nietzsche wrote that someone who has a "why" can endure almost any "how." A study shows that students who connect their homework to a larger purpose (helping, learning) persevere more when faced with a boring task.
cards.action: Try it today: write down why a difficult task matters to you.

source.nom: Gollwitzer & Sheeran, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006

rappel.q: What type of sentence helps to take action?

cards.titre: The phrase "If..., then..." helps to keep one's resolutions.
cards.texte: "If it's 6 p.m., then I'll do 10 minutes of exercise." Planning the situation and the action in advance prevents hesitation when the time comes. A meta-analysis of 94 studies shows a clear effect on goal achievement.
cards.action: Try it today: write a "If..., then..." sentence for something you are putting off.

source.nom: Francesco Cirillo, technique dite Pomodoro (marque déposée)

rappel.q: How long does a work period last?

cards.titre: The 25-minute method
cards.texte: Work for 25 minutes without your phone, then take a 5-minute break. Breaking a large task down into smaller chunks makes it less daunting. It's often called the Pomodoro Technique, named after a tomato-shaped timer.
cards.action: Try it today: spend 25 minutes on an assignment.

source.nom: Hillman et al., Neuroscience, 2009

rappel.q: How many minutes of walking were included in the study?

cards.titre: Walking for 20 minutes helps with concentration
cards.texte: In one study, children who walked for 20 minutes performed better on an attention and reading test than those who remained seated. Movement stimulates the brain.
cards.action: Try this today: walk for 20 minutes before starting your homework.

source.nom: Milkman, Minson & Volpp, Management Science, 2014

rappel.q: When did they listen to their audiobook?

cards.titre: Associating a chore with a pleasure helps to get started.
cards.texte: Researchers asked people to listen to their favorite audiobook only at the gym. They went more often. This is called "combining temptations."
cards.action: Try it today: choose a pleasure that you only allow yourself during a chore.

source.nom: Scullin et al., Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2018

rappel.q: What should I write before going to sleep?

cards.titre: Writing down your list for tomorrow helps you fall asleep.
cards.texte: In one study, people who spent 5 minutes writing their to-do list for the next day fell asleep faster than those who wrote about what they had already done.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, write down 3 things to do tomorrow before you go to bed.

source.nom: Ranehill et al., Psychological Science, 2015

rappel.q: What do studies on posture show?

cards.titre: Standing up straight can help you feel more confident.
cards.texte: Adopting an open posture for a few minutes can boost confidence. However, the effect on stress hormones predicted in 2010 has not been confirmed by subsequent studies. The body can help boost morale, but it's not a miracle cure.
cards.action: Try this today: before a stressful moment, stand up straight for 2 minutes with your shoulders open.

source.nom: Gilbert, Compassion Focused Therapy, 2009

rappel.q: Where can the critical voice come from?

cards.titre: The critical inner voice is not yours
cards.texte: The inner voice that says "you won't succeed" may be repeating phrases heard elsewhere, sometimes from childhood. Noticing it and asking yourself where it comes from helps you gain perspective. You can choose how you talk to yourself.
cards.action: Try it today: when your critical little voice speaks, answer it as you would a friend.

source.nom: Breines & Chen, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2012 ; Neff, 2003

rappel.q: What helps the most after a failure?

cards.titre: Self-compassion is more effective than criticism for making progress
cards.texte: Kristin Neff (University of Texas) studies self-compassion. Treating oneself with kindness after a failure helps one bounce back: in one study, students encouraged to practice self-compassion revised for longer after a failure.
cards.action: Try it today: after making a mistake, tell yourself what you would say to a friend.

source.nom: Bravata et al., Journal of General Internal Medicine, 2020 (revue)

rappel.q: Is imposter syndrome rare?

cards.titre: Imposter syndrome is very common
cards.texte: Many people feel less competent than they appear. Studies show that a large portion of the population experiences this at some point in their lives. Famous people like Maya Angelou have also described it.
cards.action: Try it today: tell someone about a time when you felt "out of place".

source.nom: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, JPSP, 2000

rappel.q: Do others notice us as much as we think?

cards.titre: The way others see you that you imagine is often wrong
cards.texte: The spotlight effect: we overestimate the attention others pay to us. In one study, students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt thought that about half the room had noticed it. In reality, it was about a quarter.
cards.action: Try it today: do a small thing that bothers you a little, like raising your hand.

source.nom: Bandura, Self-efficacy, 1977 (expériences de maîtrise)

rappel.q: What builds trust?

cards.titre: Acting before being confident builds confidence, not the other way around.
cards.texte: We often wait until we're ready to act, but confidence is born primarily from experience. According to Albert Bandura, every challenge met, even imperfectly, strengthens the feeling of being capable.
cards.action: Try it today: do something today that you don't feel ready for yet.

source.nom: Gross, Emotion Regulation, 2015

rappel.q: What prolongs an emotion?

cards.titre: An emotion that isn't nurtured eventually fades away.
cards.texte: A strong emotion rises and then falls. What makes it last are often the thoughts we add to it. Observing it without judgment, while breathing, helps it pass more quickly.
cards.action: Try this today: the next time a strong emotion arises, observe it without judging it.

source.nom: Lieberman et al., Psychological Science, 2007

rappel.q: What happens when you name an emotion?
choix: It helps to calm her down.

cards.titre: Naming an emotion helps to calm it.
cards.texte: Putting words to what you're feeling ("affect labeling") activates areas of the brain that regulate and reduces the activity of the amygdala, which is linked to alarm. Saying "I'm anxious" already helps a little to calm down.
cards.action: Try this today: when you feel bad, put a specific word to your emotion.

source.nom: Emmons & McCullough, JPSP, 2003 ; Seligman et al., American Psychologist, 2005

rappel.q: What should I do each evening according to this map?

cards.titre: Noting what's going well trains your attention
cards.texte: Writing down three positive things about your day each evening can slightly improve your mood over the course of several weeks, according to several studies. The brain also gets used to noticing what's going well.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, write down 3 positive things from your day.

source.nom: Lee et al., PNAS, 2019

rappel.q: How much more did the most optimistic people live on?

cards.titre: Optimism is associated with a longer life
cards.texte: A Harvard study of approximately 70,000 women and 1,400 men observed that the most optimistic individuals lived on average 11 to 15% longer. This is a statistical correlation; it does not prove that optimism is the sole cause.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, imagine something that could very well happen tomorrow.

source.nom: Kross et al., JPSP, 2014

rappel.q: What word should we use to talk to ourselves with perspective?

cards.titre: Talk to yourself like you would to a friend
cards.texte: Using first names ("Léa, you can do it") instead of "I" helps to create distance. Studies have shown that this reduces anxiety before public speaking.
cards.action: Try it today: encourage yourself once today using your first name.

source.nom: Boothby et al., Psychological Science, 2018

rappel.q: What do we underestimate after a conversation?

cards.titre: Other people appreciate you more than you think.
cards.texte: After an initial conversation, people almost always underestimate how much the other person liked them. Researchers call this the "sympathy gap".
cards.action: Try it today: start a conversation with someone you don't know very well.

source.nom: Zhao & Epley, Psychological Science, 2021

rappel.q: How do we react to a compliment?

cards.titre: A compliment is more appreciated than you might think.
cards.texte: Studies have shown that people thought their compliment would make the other person uncomfortable. In reality, those who received it were much happier than expected.
cards.action: Try it today: Give someone a sincere and specific compliment today.

source.nom: Gross & John, JPSP, 2003 (suppression émotionnelle)

rappel.q: What does this card advise for anger?

cards.titre: Hiding your emotions constantly is not good for you
cards.texte: Studies suggest that chronically suppressing emotions is linked to increased stress and less satisfying relationships. Expressing them calmly, with words, is a better strategy.
cards.action: Try this today: calmly tell someone something that has annoyed you.

source.nom: Gračanin, Bylsma & Vingerhoets, Frontiers in Psychology, 2014

rappel.q: What do studies say about tears?

cards.titre: Crying can help you feel better
cards.texte: Some studies suggest that crying helps you calm down and attracts support from others. It has also been said that tears release stress hormones, but this has not been proven. Crying is not a weakness.
cards.action: Try it today: the next time you cry, notice how you feel afterwards.

source.nom: Brooks, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014

rappel.q: What phrase is helpful before an oral exam?

cards.titre: Stress and excitement are very similar in the body
cards.texte: Rapid heartbeat, adrenaline: the body reacts almost the same way. The difference lies mainly in what we tell ourselves. In one study, people who told themselves "I'm excited" performed better in their speeches.
cards.action: Try it today: before a stressful moment, tell yourself "I am excited".

source.nom: Weisz & Zaki, Current Opinion in Psychology, 2018

rappel.q: How to strengthen empathy?
choix: Putting yourself in someone else's shoes

cards.titre: Empathy can be learned and strengthened
cards.texte: Empathy is not something we are born with. Studies show that it can be trained, for example by practicing imagining what the other person is feeling and by truly listening to them.
cards.action: Try this today: imagine an argument from the other person's point of view.

source.nom: Zaccaro et al., Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 2018 (revue)

rappel.q: Which part of breathing lasts the longest?

cards.titre: Your breathing is a tool to calm yourself down.
cards.texte: You can't slow your heart rate on command, but you can control your breathing. Exhaling for longer than you inhale (4 seconds, then 6) activates mechanisms that help the body slow down.
cards.action: Try this today: take 5 breaths: 4 seconds to inhale, 6 to exhale.

source.nom: Holt-Lunstad et al., PLoS Medicine, 2010 ; Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2015

rappel.q: What is social connection, according to this map?

cards.titre: Loneliness takes a toll on health
cards.texte: Meta-analyses by Julianne Holt-Lunstad, involving hundreds of thousands of people, link social isolation to a higher risk of mortality, comparable, according to her, to factors such as smoking. Social connection is a need, not a luxury.
cards.action: Try it today: send a message to someone you haven't contacted in a long time.

source.nom: Zatorre, Chen & Penhune, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2007

rappel.q: What does playing an instrument involve?

cards.titre: Playing music makes the whole brain work
cards.texte: Playing an instrument simultaneously engages hearing, motor skills, vision, and emotions. Musicians who started young often show measurable differences in certain brain connections.
cards.action: Try this today: listen to a piece of music while trying to follow only one instrument.

source.nom: Hunter, Gillespie & Chen, Frontiers in Psychology, 2019

rappel.q: How long in the wild, according to the study?

cards.titre: 20 minutes in nature reduces cortisol by 21%
cards.texte: A study from the University of Michigan measured that a 20-30 minute outing in a natural setting lowers cortisol, a stress hormone, faster than its natural decline during the day.
cards.action: Try this today: walk outside for 20 minutes, without your phone.

source.nom: Gross, Emotion Regulation, 2015

rappel.q: What should you do before reacting to an emotion?

cards.titre: An emotion rises and then falls
cards.texte: An emotion is like a wave: it rises, then falls if it isn't nurtured with thoughts. Letting a few seconds pass before reacting often prevents regretting one's words.
cards.action: Try this today: when an emotion arises, breathe and count to 10 before reacting.

source.nom: Neff, Self and Identity, 2003 ; Breines & Chen, 2012

rappel.q: What helps you bounce back the most?

cards.titre: Self-compassion improves performance more than self-criticism.
cards.texte: Kristin Neff (University of Texas) has shown that people who treat themselves kindly after a failure recover more easily and learn better from their mistakes than those who criticize themselves harshly.
cards.action: Try it today: write a kind sentence that you would say to yourself after a failure.

source.nom: Seligman et al., American Psychologist, 2005

rappel.q: How many positive things should you note down each day?

cards.titre: Keeping a gratitude journal can improve mood
cards.texte: In one study, noting down three things that went well each evening improved participants' mood for several months. The attention we pay to things influences how we experience our day.
cards.action: Try it today: write the name of someone you thank today and why.

source.nom: Hölzel, Lazar et al., Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 2010

rappel.q: How many weeks did the practice under study last?

cards.titre: Meditation can change the brain
cards.texte: A study by Sara Lazar's team (Harvard) observed that after 8 weeks of meditation, the decrease in perceived stress was accompanied by a reduction in the density of the amygdala, an area linked to fear. It was a small study and needs to be confirmed.
cards.action: Try it today: sit for 3 minutes and simply observe your breathing.

source.nom: Harlow, 1958 ; Field, Touch, 2014

rappel.q: What hormone does touch release?

cards.titre: Physical contact heals things that words cannot reach
cards.texte: Babies deprived of physical contact do not develop as well, even if they are well-fed. Gentle touch releases oxytocin, helps to calm them, and strengthens the bond.
cards.action: Try it today: give a hug or a friendly pat to someone you love.

source.nom: Keltner & Gross, fonctions des émotions, 1999

rappel.q: What does sadness often signal?

cards.titre: Sadness signals what really matters to you.
cards.texte: We feel sad about things that matter to us. Avoiding it only postpones dealing with it. Listening to it, identifying what it's saying ("I've lost something precious") allows us to get through it.
cards.action: Try this today: when you're sad, ask yourself, "What matters to me here?"

source.nom: Coles et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2022

rappel.q: What is this hypothesis called?

cards.titre: The face influences emotions to some extent.
cards.texte: According to the facial feedback hypothesis, facial muscles send signals to the brain. A large international study from 2022 suggests that a forced smile slightly improves mood, but the effect is small and still debated.
cards.action: Try this today: hold a pencil between your teeth for 30 seconds and note if your mood changes.

source.nom: Werner & Smith, étude longitudinale de Kauai (1955-1995)

rappel.q: What helped the children of Kauai the most?

cards.titre: Resilience is built, it is not inherited.
cards.texte: The Kauai study (Emmy Werner): children in severe difficulty became resilient if they had at least one trusted, caring adult. Just one. Resilience is relational.
cards.action: Try it today: think of an adult who mattered to you, and tell them thank you.

source.nom: Pennebaker & Beall, Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 1986

rappel.q: How long did the participants write for?

cards.titre: Writing about what hurts can be beneficial.
cards.texte: James Pennebaker (Texas) asked students to write for 15 to 20 minutes about a difficult event, several days in a row. They then visited the doctor less frequently. The benefits are modest but have been observed in numerous studies.
cards.action: Try it today: write for 10 minutes about what's bothering you, then put the paper away.

source.nom: Mann & Cadman, Creativity Research Journal, 2014

rappel.q: What can boredom lead to?

cards.titre: Boredom is not a problem — it's a compass
cards.texte: Psychologist Sandi Mann has shown that people who have just completed a boring task subsequently come up with more creative ideas. Boredom signals a need for something different and can encourage exploration.
cards.action: Try it today: stay 5 minutes without a screen and write down the ideas that come to you.

source.nom: Yoo et al., Current Biology, 2007

rappel.q: What effect does lack of sleep have on emotions?

cards.titre: A sleepless night makes emotions stronger
cards.texte: After a sleepless night, the amygdala, the area of the brain that responds to emotions, reacted about 60% more strongly in one study. It's not that you're "too sensitive": it's the fatigue.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, go to bed 20 minutes earlier.

source.nom: Hatfield, Cacioppo & Rapson, Emotional Contagion, 1994

rappel.q: What is the name of this phenomenon?

cards.titre: Emotions spread like a cold.
cards.texte: We unconsciously imitate the expressions and tone of others, and end up feeling a bit the same thing. It's emotional contagion: good humor is contagious too.
cards.action: Try it today: walk into a room with a big smile and observe the effect.

source.nom: Kumar & Epley, Psychological Science, 2018

rappel.q: Who underestimates the effect of a thank you?

cards.titre: A thank you message has a greater impact than you might think.
cards.texte: Researchers asked people to write a thank-you letter. Those who received it were much happier, and less embarrassed, than the authors had imagined.
cards.action: Try it today: send a specific thank you message to someone.

source.nom: Attribuée à Germaine de Staël

rappel.q: To whom is this phrase attributed?

cards.titre: Politeness is the art of choosing among one's thoughts
cards.texte: A quote attributed to Germaine de Staël: Not all our thoughts deserve to be spoken. Politeness is choosing those that do good rather than those that hurt.
cards.action: Try this today: before making a criticism, ask yourself if it really helps.

source.nom: Benjamin Disraeli, discours de 1872

rappel.q: According to Disraeli, what is the secret to success?

cards.titre: The secret to success is consistency in the goal
cards.texte: Benjamin Disraeli — Not perfection in the means, but fidelity to the direction. Consistency surpasses talent over time. A course held, even slowly, is achieved.
cards.action: Try it today: choose a goal and take one tiny step towards it today.

source.nom: Pensée attribuée à Confucius ; Ésope, Le Lièvre et la Tortue

rappel.q: According to this line of thinking, what matters?

cards.titre: The important thing is not speed, but not stopping.
cards.texte: A thought attributed to Confucius. As in Aesop's fable, the tortoise that moves forward without stopping overtakes the hare that pauses. Steady progress, even small, is better than sprints followed by setbacks.
cards.action: Try today: take a small step forward today on a project, however tiny.

source.nom: Règle d’or, présente dans de nombreuses traditions (Confucius, Évangiles, Talmud…)

rappel.q: What is this rule called?

cards.titre: Treat others as you would like to be treated
cards.texte: This idea is called the "golden rule." It can be found in various forms in the writings of Confucius, the Bible, the Talmud, Islam, Buddhism, and the Greek philosophers. For over 2,500 years, many traditions have arrived at the same idea.
cards.action: Try it today: do for someone one thing you would like them to do for you.

source.nom: Melody Beattie, auteure américaine (« Gratitude turns what we have into enough »)

rappel.q: What is true wealth here?

cards.titre: Gratitude makes what we have enough for us.
cards.texte: An idea from American author Melody Beattie. Wealth isn't about always having more, but about appreciating what you have. Gratitude helps you avoid feeling lack.
cards.action: Try it today: name 3 things you already have that make you happy.

source.nom: Proverbe populaire

rappel.q: Where does wisdom begin here?

cards.titre: Self-respect is the beginning of wisdom
cards.texte: Popular proverb: To respect others, you must also respect yourself. Self-esteem is not pride; it is the foundation of healthy relationships.
cards.action: Try it today: tell yourself one quality you have, out loud.

source.nom: Attribuée à Vincent Van Gogh, lettre à son frère Théo (1882)

rappel.q: To whom is this phrase attributed?

cards.titre: Great things are accomplished through a series of small things.
cards.texte: Van Gogh — The cathedral is built brick by brick. Mastery comes hour by hour. Impulse creates the spark; discipline builds the work.
cards.action: Try this today: break down a large job into 3 small steps and do the first one.

source.nom: Pensée attribuée à Sénèque

rappel.q: To whom is this thought attributed?

cards.titre: What you think of yourself is more important than what others think.
cards.texte: A thought attributed to Seneca. The opinion that most influences your life is the one you have of yourself: it filters everything that others say.
cards.action: Try it today: write one thing you think is good about yourself.

source.nom: Pensée attribuée à Lao Tseu ; phrase attribuée à Thomas Edison

rappel.q: What can we learn from a failed attempt?

cards.titre: Failure is the foundation of success
cards.texte: A thought attributed to Lao Tzu. Every failed attempt shows what doesn't work. Thomas Edison is credited with this saying: "I haven't failed, I've just found 1,000 ways that won't work."
cards.action: Try this today: think back to a recent mistake and write down what you learned from it.

source.nom: Steve Jobs, discours à l’université Stanford, 2005

rappel.q: Where did Steve Jobs say that?

cards.titre: The only way to do good work is to love what you do.
cards.texte: Steve Jobs, Stanford commencement address (2005). Desire is not a luxury, it's fuel. People who excel have discipline, but they've also found something they're passionate about.
cards.action: Try this today: write an activity that makes you forget about the time.

source.nom: Idée centrale de la tradition bouddhiste et du stoïcisme

rappel.q: Where does suffering often come from, according to this line of thought?

cards.titre: Inner peace begins when we stop wanting things to be different
cards.texte: This philosophy is inspired by Buddhism. It's not about resignation, but about accepting what is. Suffering often stems from a denial of reality. Acceptance frees up energy to change what can be changed.
cards.action: Try this today: think of one thing you cannot change, and let it go for today.

source.nom: Proverbe dit grec (origine incertaine)

rappel.q: What are we doing by planting these trees?

cards.titre: Plant trees whose shade you will never see
cards.texte: Greek proverb — The best actions are often those from which we will not benefit. Educating, protecting, building for those who come after. That is the definition of civilization.
cards.action: Try it today: do one useful thing for someone who will come after you.

source.nom: Inscription du temple d’Apollon à Delphes, reprise par Socrate (Platon)

rappel.q: Where was this sentence written?

cards.titre: Know thyself
cards.texte: Inscribed at the Temple of Delphi and later adopted by Socrates: Knowing oneself means knowing what frightens us, what makes us strong, and what we don't see in ourselves. This helps us make better choices.
cards.action: Try it today: write down one of your strengths and one of your fears.

source.nom: Pensée populaire (attribution incertaine)

rappel.q: What does knowledge do when it is given?

cards.titre: The only wealth that grows by sharing is knowledge.
cards.texte: Popular belief: Unlike money, knowledge doesn't diminish when shared. By explaining something, you even understand it better yourself.
cards.action: Try it today: explain to someone something you learned today.

source.nom: Dhammapada, verset 1 (texte bouddhiste ancien)

rappel.q: From which text does this idea originate?

cards.titre: What we are is the result of what we have thought
cards.texte: First verse of the Dhammapada, an ancient Buddhist text. The mind is like a garden: the thoughts we cultivate become habits, and habits shape our character.
cards.action: Try it today: notice a thought that comes back often and ask yourself if it helps you.

source.nom: Héraclite, fragments (via Platon, Cratyle)

rappel.q: Who said that?

cards.titre: You never step into the same river twice.
cards.texte: Heraclitus — Everything changes, nothing lasts. Even you have changed since yesterday. True wisdom lies in accepting change rather than fighting it.
cards.action: Try it today: write down one thing that has changed about you since last year.

source.nom: Proverbe populaire, souvent dit chinois (origine incertaine)

rappel.q: What better thing to do than curse the darkness?

cards.titre: It is better to light a candle than to curse the darkness
cards.texte: Chinese proverb — Complaining about a situation doesn't change it. Seeking the smallest possible action to improve it, even a symbolic one, changes both the environment and the state of mind.
cards.action: Try this today: when faced with a problem, take the smallest possible action to improve it.

source.nom: Nelson Mandela, Un long chemin vers la liberté, 1994 (idée paraphrasée)

rappel.q: According to Mandela, what is courage?

cards.titre: Courage is not the absence of fear, it is acting in spite of it.
cards.texte: Nelson Mandela's idea: Everyone is afraid. The courageous are not those who feel nothing, but those who act despite their fear.
cards.action: Try it today: do something that scares you a little but is safe.

source.nom: Pensée populaire (souvent attribuée à divers auteurs)

rappel.q: What is a book according to this line of thought?

cards.titre: Books are friends who never betray you
cards.texte: Popular belief: A book is a conversation with someone who knows more, available at any time and without judgment. Some books change our perspective forever.
cards.action: Try it today: read 10 pages of a book you like.

source.nom: Anaïs Nin, La Séduction du Minotaure, 1961 (idée reprise du Talmud)

rappel.q: How do we see things according to this idea?

cards.titre: We don't see things as they are, we see them as we are.
cards.texte: Anaïs Nin — Two people who experience the same event perceive it differently according to their history, their fears, their desires. Changing perspective changes reality.
cards.action: Try it today: ask someone how they experienced a moment you shared.

source.nom: Pensée inspirée de l’existentialisme de Jean-Paul Sartre

rappel.q: What is freedom according to this line of thought?

cards.titre: Freedom is choosing your chains
cards.texte: A thought inspired by Jean-Paul Sartre. All life involves constraints. Freedom is not the absence of commitment, but consciously choosing one's commitments rather than passively accepting them.
cards.action: Try it today: choose a commitment that you truly decided on, not one that was imposed upon you.

source.nom: Nicolas Boileau, L’Art poétique, 1674

rappel.q: Who wrote this sentence?

cards.titre: What is clearly conceived is clearly expressed
cards.texte: Nicolas Boileau, The Art of Poetry (1674). If you can't explain something simply, it's perhaps because you haven't fully understood it yet. Clear thinking leads to clear words.
cards.action: Try it today: explain a lesson in 3 simple sentences.

source.nom: Sénèque, De brevitate vitae, I (traduction PocketSage depuis le latin)

rappel.q: According to Seneca, what is the problem?

cards.titre: We don't have a little time, we waste a lot of it
cards.texte: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life (1st century). "Non exiguum temporis habemus, sed multum perdidimus": life is long enough if one knows how to use it.
cards.action: Try it today: write down an activity that took up your time without bringing you any pleasure.

source.nom: Épictète, Manuel, 1 (traduction PocketSage depuis le grec)

rappel.q: Where should we put our energy, according to Epictetus?

cards.titre: Some things depend on you, others do not.
cards.texte: Epictetus, a former slave turned philosopher, begins his Manual thus: our judgments, our desires, and our actions depend on us; the weather or the opinions of others do not. Put your energy into the former.
cards.action: Try this today: make two columns: "depends on me" and "does not depend on me".

source.nom: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, livre VI, fable 10 (1668)

rappel.q: Why does the tortoise win?

cards.titre: There's no point in rushing; you have to leave on time.
cards.texte: Jean de La Fontaine, The Hare and the Tortoise (1668). The tortoise wins because it starts on time and does not stop, while the hare, too sure of itself, lags behind.
cards.action: Try today: start today a small part of a job planned for later.

source.nom: Marc Aurèle, Pensées, X, 16 (traduction PocketSage depuis le grec)

rappel.q: What did Marcus Aurelius advise?

cards.titre: Stop debating what constitutes a good person: just be one.
cards.texte: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (Book X). The philosopher-emperor recalled that it is better to act kindly than to debate endlessly about kindness.
cards.action: Try this today: do a kind deed instead of talking about it.

source.nom: Smithsonian’s National Zoo, Asian elephant ; McComb et al., Science, 2001

rappel.q: What does an elephant find years later?

cards.titre: Elephants have an extraordinary memory
cards.texte: An elephant remembers the faces of its friends and the paths it has traveled for a long time. It can find a watering hole, even very far away, many years later.
cards.action: Try it today: close your eyes and find your way back to your room in your mind.

source.nom: NOAA Fisheries ; Rattenborg et al., 2000 (sommeil unihémisphérique)

rappel.q: How do dolphins sleep?

cards.titre: Dolphins sleep with only one eye open
cards.texte: Half of their brain sleeps while the other half stays awake to breathe and watch for danger. They can even swim while sleeping!
cards.action: Try it today: close one eye, then the other: you can't sleep like a dolphin!

source.nom: Encyclopédie, radula des gastéropodes

rappel.q: Where are the snail's teeth?

cards.titre: A snail has thousands of teeth… on its tongue!
cards.texte: Its tongue is called a radula. It is covered with thousands of tiny teeth that scrape plants. And the snail moves very slowly, leaving a trail of slime to glide along.
cards.action: Try it today: touch your tongue: it's soft, not full of teeth!

source.nom: NOAA SciJinks, rainbows ; optique de base

rappel.q: What shape does a rainbow really have?

cards.titre: The rainbow is actually a complete circle
cards.texte: From the sky, it would appear whole and round. From the ground, the earth hides half of it. Sunlight hides in each raindrop and emerges divided into all its colors.
cards.action: Try this today: after the rain, look for a rainbow with the sun at your back.

source.nom: NASA Science, Moon Facts

rappel.q: Where does the light of the Moon come from?

cards.titre: The moon shines but does not produce light
cards.texte: It reflects sunlight, like a giant mirror. Without the Sun, the Moon would be completely black in the sky. And it moves away from Earth by almost 4 cm every year.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, look at the Moon and find the side illuminated by the Sun.

source.nom: Smithsonian, Butterflies taste with their feet

rappel.q: What does the butterfly taste?

cards.titre: Butterflies taste with their legs
cards.texte: As soon as they land on a flower, their feet can sense if it's good, even before their mouths touch it. They have taste receptors at the tips of their feet!
cards.action: Try it today: taste a fruit with your eyes closed and guess which one it is.

source.nom: NOAA Ocean Service, How much water is in the ocean? ; fosse des Mariannes (NOAA)

rappel.q: What covers the most of the Earth?

cards.titre: The ocean covers more than half of the Earth
cards.texte: If you looked at the Earth from space, you would mostly see blue water. The oceans are so deep that the world's highest mountain (Everest) would fit inside them.
cards.action: Try it today: look at a globe or a world map: count the blue areas.

source.nom: Smithsonian’s National Zoo, American flamingo

rappel.q: Why are flamingos pink?

cards.titre: Flamingos are born grey-white
cards.texte: Baby flamingos are grey or white. Their pink color comes from what they eat: small shrimp and algae full of pigments. Without this food, they would gradually lose their color.
cards.action: Try this today: eat a colorful food and say its color.

source.nom: NASA Space Place, light-years

rappel.q: What do we see when we look at a star?

cards.titre: When you look at a star, you are looking at the past
cards.texte: It takes years, sometimes thousands of years, for the light from a star to reach us. So you see the star as it was a very long time ago.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, look for the brightest star in the sky.

source.nom: Simard et al., Nature, 1997

rappel.q: What connects the roots of trees?

cards.titre: The trees speak silently beneath the earth
cards.texte: Underground, tree roots are connected by tiny fungi. These fungi transport water and nutrients from one tree to another. Scientists are still studying how trees help each other in this way.
cards.action: Try this today: in the park, touch the bark of a tree and look for mushrooms at its base.

source.nom: NOAA Fisheries, Blue Whale

rappel.q: What is the largest animal that ever existed?

cards.titre: The blue whale is the largest animal that ever lived
cards.texte: She is bigger than all the dinosaurs! Her heart is as big as a small car. Her baby already weighs 2 to 3 tons at birth, as much as 30 adults.
cards.action: Try it today: count how many adults it would take to weigh as much as a baby whale.

source.nom: Smithsonian Magazine, The Science Behind Honey’s Eternal Shelf Life (2013)

rappel.q: Why does honey keep for so long?

cards.titre: Honey never spoils, even after 3,000 years
cards.texte: Archaeologists have found honey over 3,000 years old in Egyptian tombs, still well preserved! The honey has very little water and is slightly acidic: microbes cannot live in it.
cards.action: Try this today: look at a jar of honey and observe how thick it is.

source.nom: NOAA Fisheries, Sea Otter ; Monterey Bay Aquarium

rappel.q: Why do otters hold each other's paws?

cards.titre: Sea otters hold hands to sleep
cards.texte: When they sleep on the water, otters hold onto each other's paws. That way, the waves don't separate them. Sometimes, they also wrap themselves in seaweed, like in a blanket!
cards.action: Try this today: give someone an otter hug before going to sleep.

source.nom: NOAA Ocean Service, Are starfish really fish?

rappel.q: What doesn't a starfish have?

cards.titre: The starfish has no brain
cards.texte: It has neither a brain nor blood! Nerves in each of its arms help it to move. And instead of blood, it uses seawater.
cards.action: Try this today: draw a starfish and count its arms.

source.nom: Encyclopédie, anatomie des crevettes (céphalothorax)

rappel.q: Where is the heart of the shrimp?

cards.titre: The heart of the shrimp is in its head
cards.texte: In shrimp, the heart is located just behind the eyes, in the part we call the head. Its body is not arranged like ours!
cards.action: Try it today: place your hand on your heart: it's in your chest, not in your head!

source.nom: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Koala

rappel.q: How many hours does a koala sleep?

cards.titre: The koala sleeps almost all day
cards.texte: A koala can sleep 18 to 22 hours a day! The eucalyptus leaves it eats give it very little energy, so it rests a lot.
cards.action: Try it today: count how many hours you sleep, and compare with the koala.

source.nom: Smithsonian’s National Zoo, Giraffe

rappel.q: How many bones are in a giraffe's neck?

cards.titre: The giraffe has as many bones in its neck as you
cards.texte: Its neck is huge, but it has 7 bones, just like yours! In giraffes, each bone is simply much longer.
cards.action: Try it today: touch your neck and imagine it's as long as a giraffe's.

source.nom: Smithsonian Ocean, Octopus ; Monterey Bay Aquarium

rappel.q: Why does the octopus change color?

cards.titre: The octopus changes color in the blink of an eye
cards.texte: Her skin contains thousands of tiny colored pockets. She can turn red, white, or mottled in a second to hide or show that she is unhappy.
cards.action: Try it today: play hide-and-seek by standing in front of a color close to your clothes.

source.nom: Euronews, 16/04/2025 ; Te Papa Museum

rappel.q: Which animal has the biggest eyes?

cards.titre: The colossal squid has eyes the size of a dinner plate
cards.texte: Its eyes measure approximately 27 cm: they are the largest in the animal kingdom. In the darkness of the deep sea, they capture the faintest glimmer of light. It was filmed alive for the first time only in 2025.
cards.action: Try this today: draw an eye the size of a plate next to your eye.

source.nom: NASA Earth Observatory ; mesures GPS de l’Himalaya

rappel.q: What is driving Everest upwards?

cards.titre: Mount Everest is still growing by a few millimeters per year.
cards.texte: The tectonic plates of India and Asia continue to push against each other, causing the Himalayas to rise a few millimeters each year. At the same time, wind and rain erode the mountains. These two forces have been battling for millions of years.
cards.action: Try it today: measure 4 mm on a ruler: that's what Everest gains per year.

source.nom: NOAA NCEI, World Magnetic Model

rappel.q: What moves every year?

cards.titre: The Earth is a giant magnet with poles that move.
cards.texte: The magnetic North Pole is moving: in recent decades, it has shifted by up to 50 km per year, towards Russia. Our grandparents' compasses therefore pointed to a slightly different location.
cards.action: Try this today: make a compass with a magnetized needle on a cork in water.

source.nom: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology, 2016

rappel.q: How many bacteria are there per human cell?

cards.titre: Your body contains roughly as many bacteria as cells
cards.texte: Approximately 38 trillion bacteria live inside you, mostly in your gut, compared to about 30 trillion human cells. It used to be said "ten times more," but that was a mistake. Most of these bacteria help you digest food.
cards.action: Try it today: eat a yogurt and think about the good bacteria that live in you.

source.nom: USGS, Inside the Earth

rappel.q: What is the Earth's mantle like in particular?

cards.titre: Beneath the crust, the rock moves very slowly
cards.texte: The Earth's crust is 5 to 70 km thick. Below it, the mantle is very hot, but above all, it is solid: it deforms very slowly, like dough, over millions of years. Magma only forms in certain places.
cards.action: Try it today: warm up some modeling clay in your hands: it becomes softer, like the mantle over millions of years.

source.nom: Encyclopædia Britannica, vision des rapaces

rappel.q: How many times better does the eagle see?

cards.titre: Eagles can see 4 to 5 times better than humans
cards.texte: It can spot a rabbit from over 3 km away. Its eyes are enormous for its head: if ours were as large in proportion, they would be the size of an orange.
cards.action: Try it today: look into the distance and try to spot the smallest detail possible.

source.nom: NASA Science, Sun Facts

rappel.q: How many Earths would fit inside the Sun?

cards.titre: The sun is so big that 1.3 million Earths would fit inside it.
cards.texte: And yet, the Sun is a fairly ordinary star among the 100 to 400 billion stars in our galaxy. Some giant stars are more than 1,000 times larger than it.
cards.action: Try it today: compare a marble and a balloon: it's a bit like the Earth next to the Sun.

source.nom: Encyclopædia Britannica, allotropes du carbone

rappel.q: What are diamond and graphite made of?

cards.titre: Diamonds come from the same material as the pencil
cards.texte: Both are pure carbon. In a diamond, the atoms are tightly bound in all directions. In the graphite of a pencil, they form layers that slide. Same atoms, different arrangement, opposite results.
cards.action: Try it today: look at the lead of your pencil: it's carbon, like a diamond.

source.nom: USGS, Water Density

rappel.q: Why does ice float?

cards.titre: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
cards.texte: Almost all materials are denser in solid form than in liquid form. Not water. This anomaly is vital: if the ice were to flow, the lakes would freeze from the bottom up and kill all aquatic life.
cards.action: Try it today: put an ice cube in a glass of water and watch it float.

source.nom: Encyclopédie, nyctinastie ; Darwin, The Power of Movement in Plants, 1880

rappel.q: What is the name of this nocturnal movement?

cards.titre: Plants go to sleep at night
cards.texte: Many plants fold their leaves or flowers at sunset — this is called nyctinasty. They have a circadian rhythm like us. Some can even anticipate dawn.
cards.action: Try this today: observe a houseplant in the morning and evening.

source.nom: NOAA Ocean Service, How much oxygen comes from the ocean?

rappel.q: What produces half of the oxygen?

cards.titre: One out of every two breaths comes from the ocean
cards.texte: Tiny algae floating in the sea, called phytoplankton, produce about half of the Earth's oxygen. You owe one out of every two breaths you take to the ocean!
cards.action: Try it today: take 2 deep breaths and say thank you to the ocean for the second one.

source.nom: NASA Space Place, How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?

rappel.q: How long does it take for sunlight to reach the Earth?

cards.titre: Sunlight is 8 minutes behind
cards.texte: It takes light about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to us. The Sun you see is the one from 8 minutes ago.
cards.action: Try it today: set an 8-minute timer: that's the time it takes for light to travel.

source.nom: Karl von Frisch, prix Nobel 1973

rappel.q: What does the dance of the bee indicate?

cards.titre: The bees dance to give the address of the flowers
cards.texte: Upon returning to the hive, the bee performs a figure-eight dance. The angle of the dance indicates the direction of the flowers, and its duration indicates the distance.
cards.action: Try this today: invent a dance to show someone where an object is hidden.

source.nom: NASA Science, Mars Facts

rappel.q: Approximately how long is a day on Mars?

cards.titre: A day on Mars lasts 40 minutes longer
cards.texte: Mars rotates on its axis in just over 24 hours and 37 minutes. The teams that pilot the Martian robots adjust their alarm clocks every day to keep up with Martian time!
cards.action: Try it today: calculate what your day would be like with 40 more minutes.

source.nom: NASA Science, Olympus Mons

rappel.q: Where is the largest volcano located?

cards.titre: The largest volcano in the solar system is on Mars.
cards.texte: Olympus Mons is over 20 km high, about 2.5 times the height of Everest. It is so wide that it would cover almost all of France.
cards.action: Try it today: draw Everest and Olympus Mons side by side at the correct scale.

source.nom: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz, JPSP, 1978

rappel.q: Which word increased acceptance?

cards.titre: People prefer a bad explanation to no explanation.
cards.texte: In a famous experiment (Ellen Langer, 1978), a person asked to go to the front of the line at the photocopier. With a nonsensical reason ("because I have to make copies"), 93% agreed, compared to 60% with no reason at all. The simple "because" is reassuring.
cards.action: Try it today: notice how many times you are given a "because" without a real reason.

source.nom: Kahneman & Tversky, Econometrica, 1979

rappel.q: What is this bias called?

cards.titre: The pain of losing €100 is twice as strong as the pleasure of winning it.
cards.texte: Loss aversion (Kahneman and Tversky): losing money hurts about twice as much as the pleasure of winning the same amount. That's why ads say "don't miss out" rather than "enjoy."
cards.action: Try it today: spot an ad that plays on the fear of missing out.

source.nom: Raichle et al., PNAS, 2001 ; Beaty et al., 2016

rappel.q: Which brain network is activated during boredom?

cards.titre: Boredom lets your creative brain work
cards.texte: When we're not actively doing anything, a set of areas called the "default mode network" activates. It contributes to daydreaming, imagining the future, and connecting ideas. Filling every minute of screen time leaves less room for it.
cards.action: Try it today: take 10 minutes without your phone or music and let your mind wander.

source.nom: Encyclopædia Britannica, Athenian democracy

rappel.q: Who voted in Athens?

cards.titre: Athenian democracy excluded the majority of the inhabitants
cards.texte: In Periclean Athens, only adult men born to Athenian parents could vote. Women, slaves, and foreigners—the vast majority of the population—were excluded. The ideal and the reality are often different.
cards.action: Try it today: find out who had the right to vote in France in 1900.

source.nom: Our World in Data, Extreme poverty (Banque mondiale)

rappel.q: What has extreme poverty done since 1990?

cards.titre: Extreme poverty has declined significantly in 30 years.
cards.texte: Between 1990 and 2019, the proportion of humanity living in extreme poverty fell from approximately 36% to less than 10%, according to the World Bank. More than a billion people were lifted out of extreme poverty, largely thanks to growth in Asia.
cards.action: Try it today: go to Our World in Data and look at the extreme poverty curve.

source.nom: National Human Genome Research Institute ; Chimpanzee Sequencing Consortium, Nature, 2005

rappel.q: What proportion of DNA do two humans share?

cards.titre: 99.9% of your DNA is identical to that of any other human
cards.texte: The remaining 0.1% explains many of our differences. We also share approximately 98.8% of our DNA with chimpanzees. But beware of viral figures like "60% with a banana": they only compare certain genes, not all of our DNA.
cards.action: Try it today: count the differences between you and a friend: they are contained in 0.1% of your DNA.

source.nom: Blague classique d’esprit critique (chiffre volontairement inventé)

rappel.q: What should you ask when faced with a number?

cards.titre: 84% of the statistics cited are fabricated.
cards.texte: (This one included.) The critical thinking tool: ask for the primary source. A study conducted on whom, when, where, by whom, and funded? Figures without a source are rhetoric dressed up as fact.
cards.action: Try it today: for the next statistic you hear, look up its source.

source.nom: Marc Aurèle, Pensées pour moi-même (IIᵉ siècle)

rappel.q: For whom was Marcus Aurelius writing?

cards.titre: Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself so as not to be a tyrant
cards.texte: The "Thoughts" were never written for publication. This all-powerful emperor imposed a daily inner discipline upon himself. Reading his doubts shows that even the great struggle with themselves.
cards.action: Try it today: write 3 lines to yourself about what you want to improve.

source.nom: Raichle & Gusnard, PNAS, 2002 ; Silver et al., Science, 2018 (AlphaZero)

rappel.q: What power does the human brain use?

cards.titre: Your brain is much more energy-efficient than AI.
cards.texte: The human brain operates on about 20 watts. To learn to play chess, AlphaZero used thousands of specialized processors, and training large AI models consumes enormous amounts of electricity. In terms of efficiency, your brain remains a champion.
cards.action: Try it today: find out how much energy your own brain uses: 20 watts.

source.nom: GIEC, rapport AR6 (2021) ; Tierney et al., Nature, 2020

rappel.q: By how many degrees does the ice age differ?

cards.titre: An increase of 1.5°C is not "minor" — it's a planetary transformation.
cards.texte: The average temperature difference between the last ice age and today is approximately 5 to 6 °C. The climate does not react in a simple way: certain thresholds can trigger changes that are difficult to reverse.
cards.action: Try this today: research what a climate “tipping point” is.

source.nom: Tversky & Kahneman, Science, 1974

rappel.q: What is this bias called?

cards.titre: The first figure we heard tricks us.
cards.texte: If a seller initially advertises a price of €200, a price of €120 seems like a bargain, even if the item is worth €60. The first figure acts as an anchor for your brain: this is the anchoring effect.
cards.action: Try it today: before looking at a price, decide how much you are willing to pay.

source.nom: Johnson & Goldstein, Science, 2003

rappel.q: Why do the pre-ticked boxes work?

cards.titre: The default option often decides for us
cards.texte: In countries where organ donation must be explicitly refused, many more people are donors than in countries where registration is required. People often keep what is already checked.
cards.action: Try it today: check a "default" setting on your phone that you've never chosen.

source.nom: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, JPSP, 1994

rappel.q: What is this error called?

cards.titre: The time required is almost always underestimated.
cards.texte: Students estimated the time it would take to finish their dissertations: most exceeded even their initial "if everything goes wrong" estimate. This is the planning error.
cards.action: Try it today: take your next time estimate and add 50%.

source.nom: Wason, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1960 ; Nickerson, 1998

rappel.q: What is this bias called?

cards.titre: Our brain seeks to be right
cards.texte: We more readily seek evidence that confirms what we already believe than evidence that contradicts it. This is confirmation bias, and network algorithms amplify it.
cards.action: Try it today: find a good argument against an idea you care about.

source.nom: Sherman et al., Psychological Science, 2016

rappel.q: What do highly liked photos activate?

cards.titre: Likes activate the reward circuit
cards.texte: Researchers showed teenagers fake Instagram photos in a scanner. Photos with many likes activated more reward centers in the brain, and the teenagers were more likely to like them as well.
cards.action: Try this today: post or look at a photo without looking at the number of likes.

source.nom: Metcalfe, Annual Review of Psychology, 2017 (apprendre de ses erreurs)

rappel.q: What do the understood errors do?

cards.titre: Mistakes help your brain grow
cards.texte: When you make a mistake and understand why, new connections are created in your brain. Mistakes are not failures—they are the building blocks of learning.
cards.action: Try it today: tell us about a mistake you made and what you learned from it.

source.nom: Cepeda et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2006 (effet d’espacement)

rappel.q: What works best for learning?

cards.titre: Practicing for 10 minutes a day is better than 1 hour once a week.
cards.texte: The brain consolidates learning every night. Reviewing something several days in a row helps you memorize it much better than a single long session. A little bit each day is the secret.
cards.action: Try it today: revise for 10 minutes today, and another 10 minutes tomorrow.

source.nom: Dweck, travaux sur l’état d’esprit de croissance

rappel.q: What single word changes everything?

cards.titre: Saying "I don't know yet" changes everything
cards.texte: The word "still" transforms a failure into a path. "I don't know how to read" vs. "I don't know how to read yet" — a single syllable that says: there is a future where I will know.
cards.action: Try it today: say one thing you don't "yet" know how to do.

source.nom: Winsler, Private speech, 2009 ; Hatzigeorgiadis et al., 2011 (méta-analyse)

rappel.q: What makes people talk during a challenge?

cards.titre: Encouraging yourself out loud really works!
cards.texte: Studies on children show that talking to yourself during a challenge ("I can do it," "think calmly") improves performance. It's like having your own coach in your head.
cards.action: Try it today: during a challenge, gently tell yourself "I can do it".

source.nom: Csikszentmihalyi, Flow, 1990

rappel.q: What makes you the proudest?

cards.titre: Finding something difficult is a sign that you are learning.
cards.texte: When something is a little difficult, your brain works and grows. Succeeding at a real challenge makes you much prouder than an easy game. Challenge is what truly rewards you.
cards.action: Try it today: choose a slightly difficult game and keep trying until you succeed.

source.nom: Smithsonian, ants ; Nguyen et al., Journal of Biomechanics, 2014

rappel.q: How many times its weight can the ant carry?

cards.titre: The ant never lets go of its grain of wheat
cards.texte: An ant can carry up to 50 times its own weight, day after day. Small, quiet repetition builds great things. Your inner ant is stronger than you think!
cards.action: Try this today: carry a slightly heavy object and think about the ant.

source.nom: Jaffe, 1973 (thigmomorphogenèse)

rappel.q: What happens when a tree is shaken by the wind?

cards.titre: Trees that withstand wind have the deepest roots
cards.texte: A tree that is shaken grows stronger roots to stand. The difficulties in your life do the same: they prevent you from falling when a real storm hits.
cards.action: Try it today: plant a seed and gently blow on it every day.

source.nom: Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer, Psychological Review, 1993 (pratique délibérée)
