rappel.q: What have all champions been?

cards.titre: Before becoming good, everyone was a beginner.
cards.texte: Great athletes, musicians, and scientists all started out knowing nothing. They fell, made mistakes, and started again many times. Every expert was once a beginner.
cards.action: Try it today: ask an adult to do something they couldn't do as a child.

source.nom: Ericsson et al., 1993 (pratique)

rappel.q: What becomes of today's efforts?

cards.titre: Your efforts today are your superpowers tomorrow
cards.texte: Every time you train, you send a message to your future brain. In six months, what's hard today will be easy. And you'll remember that you persevered.
cards.action: Try it today: practice something difficult for you for 5 minutes.

source.nom: Moser et al., Psychological Science, 2011

rappel.q: What helps the brain after a mistake?

cards.titre: A mistake that is well understood leads to progress.
cards.texte: Scientists have observed that the brains of children who believe they can improve react more strongly to mistakes, and that they correct them better afterward. Mistakes, plus reflection, are the key!
cards.action: Try it today: when you make a mistake, ask yourself why.

source.nom: NOAA Fisheries, baleines (mammifères marins respirant de l’air)

rappel.q: Why does the whale swim upstream?

cards.titre: Even whales have to come up for air
cards.texte: Even the greatest creatures need breaks. Resting isn't giving up—it's recharging to dive back in stronger. Taking a break when things get tough is smart.
cards.action: Try this today: when it gets hard, take a 2-minute break and then start again.

source.nom: Encyclopédie, George de Mestral et le Velcro (1941-1955)

rappel.q: Where did the idea for Velcro come from?

cards.titre: A stupid idea can become a brilliant invention.
cards.texte: Velcro was invented by a researcher who was looking at seeds stuck to his coat. Post-it notes, Teflon, microwaves: all accidents. Your weird ideas are worth trying.
cards.action: Try it today: draw a bizarre invention that could be useful.

source.nom: Diekelmann & Born, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2010

rappel.q: What does your brain do during the night?

cards.titre: Your brain stores your lessons while you sleep
cards.texte: At night, your brain sorts what you learned during the day and stores it in your memory. Sleeping well is a bit like revising without doing anything!
cards.action: Try it today: recite your lesson when you wake up to see what your brain has stored.

source.nom: Fiorella & Mayer, Contemporary Educational Psychology, 2013

rappel.q: What happens when you explain a lesson?

cards.titre: To explain is to learn twice
cards.texte: When you explain something to someone, you understand it better yourself. That's why teachers learn so much by teaching!
cards.action: Try it today: explain to a parent something you learned today.

source.nom: Roediger & Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006

rappel.q: What helps with remembering the most?

cards.titre: Repeating without looking is the best training
cards.texte: Rereading your lesson gives the impression of knowing it. But trying to repeat it without looking at it really makes it stick in your head.
cards.action: Try it today: hide your lesson and repeat 3 things you remember.

source.nom: Adolph et al., Psychological Science, 2012

rappel.q: How many falls per hour do babies experience?

cards.titre: Babies fall 17 times an hour while learning to walk
cards.texte: Researchers filmed babies learning to walk: they fell an average of 17 times per hour! And they got back up every time. That's how they learned.
cards.action: Try this today: think of one thing you learned by making mistakes many times.

source.nom: Dewar et al., Psychological Science, 2012

rappel.q: What does a short break after a lesson do?

cards.titre: A short break helps with learning
cards.texte: After learning something, a few minutes of quiet rest with your eyes closed helps your brain to remember it better. Taking a break is part of learning!
cards.action: Try it today: after your homework, close your eyes for 3 minutes in a quiet place.

source.nom: Principe de régulation émotionnelle (Gross, 2015)

rappel.q: What does anger look like?

cards.titre: Anger is like a wave
cards.texte: Anger rises, then it subsides. If you dwell on what's upsetting you, you create another wave. But if you breathe slowly and wait, the wave passes on its own.
cards.action: Try this today: when you are angry, breathe slowly and wait for the wave to pass.

source.nom: Zaccaro et al., Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 2018

rappel.q: What needs to be done for a longer period?

cards.titre: Breathing slowly calms the body
cards.texte: Breathe out for longer than you inhale: 4 seconds to bring air in, 6 seconds to exhale. This activates a natural "brake" in your body and helps you calm down.
cards.action: Try this today: blow 3 times as if you were blowing out a candle very gently.

source.nom: Gračanin, Bylsma & Vingerhoets, Frontiers in Psychology, 2014

rappel.q: Is crying a weakness?

cards.titre: Crying can feel good.
cards.texte: After crying, many people feel calmer. Tears also show others that you need comfort. Crying is not a weakness; it's a way of expressing your feelings.
cards.action: Try this today: if you feel like crying, ask someone for a hug.

source.nom: Lieberman et al., Psychological Science, 2007

rappel.q: What should you do when you're scared?

cards.titre: Naming your fear helps it shrink
cards.texte: Scientists have discovered that putting words to what you feel helps to calm the fearful part of the brain. "I'm worried about tomorrow": just saying that sentence already helps a little.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, say the name of an emotion you experienced today.

source.nom: Light, Grewen & Amico, Biological Psychology, 2005 ; Cohen et al., Psychological Science, 2015

rappel.q: What does a hug do?

cards.titre: A hug helps you feel good
cards.texte: A warm hug helps the body release oxytocin, a hormone that calms and reassures. Hugs help us feel safe and close to the people we love.
cards.action: Try it today: give a long hug to someone you love.

source.nom: Walker & van der Helm, Psychological Bulletin, 2009

rappel.q: What effect does sleep have on emotions?
choix: It helps to calm them down.

cards.titre: Sleep is often enough to heal a deep sadness
cards.texte: During sleep, the brain "sorts out" the day's emotions. The next day, a deep sadness often hurts a little less. That's why they say: sleep brings counsel.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, before going to sleep, think of a beautiful moment from your day.

source.nom: Métaphore pédagogique courante en éducation émotionnelle

rappel.q: Do emotions last forever?

cards.titre: Emotions are like the weather — they pass
cards.texte: Dark clouds come and go. Joy, sadness, fear—none of them are permanent. When you feel bad, tell yourself: "It's just bad weather. It will pass."
cards.action: Try it today: draw your heart's weather today: sun, cloud or rain?

source.nom: Curry & Kasser, Art Therapy, 2005

rappel.q: What helps the brain to calm down?

cards.titre: Drawing or coloring calms the anxious brain
cards.texte: Calm, repetitive activities, like drawing or coloring, help many children and adults feel more relaxed. Your brain can rest from its worries.
cards.action: Try this today: color a drawing for 10 minutes in silence.

source.nom: Beetz et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2012 (revue)

rappel.q: What does petting an animal do?
choix: It puts the animal to sleep.

cards.titre: Watching an animal calms the heart
cards.texte: Studies show that petting an animal can reduce stress and help you feel better. Even looking at pictures of cute animals often puts you in a good mood!
cards.action: Try this today: gently pet an animal or look at a picture of a cute animal.

source.nom: Froh, Sefick & Emmons, Journal of School Psychology, 2008

rappel.q: How many beautiful things should I write down in the evening?

cards.titre: Saying thank you makes you happier than having more
cards.texte: Researchers asked students to write down things they were grateful for each day. After a few weeks, they felt a little happier. It's not the events themselves that change, it's what we notice.
cards.action: Try it today: tonight, say 3 nice things about your day.

source.nom: Aknin et al., PLoS ONE, 2012 (dons chez les tout-petits)

rappel.q: Who is happy when we help?

cards.titre: Helping someone makes you happy too
cards.texte: Scientists have observed that even toddlers seem happier when they give than when they receive. Doing something kind for others also makes you feel good.
cards.action: Try it today: do a small kindness for someone today.

source.nom: Trehub, chants pour bébés ; Cirelli et al., 2020

rappel.q: What makes a lullaby hum?

cards.titre: Singing or humming calms the nervous system
cards.texte: When you hum or sing softly, your breathing slows down and your body relaxes. That's also why lullabies help babies fall asleep.
cards.action: Try it today: hum your favorite song very softly.

source.nom: Psychologie des émotions : fonction de la peur (LeDoux, 1996)

rappel.q: What is the purpose of fear?

cards.titre: Fear is a bodyguard
cards.texte: Fear isn't inherently bad: it serves to protect you from danger. Sometimes, however, it's wrong and triggers false alarms, like an overly sensitive one.
cards.action: Try this today: think of a fear and ask yourself: real danger or false alarm?

source.nom: Technique de respiration rythmée d’usage courant ; Zaccaro et al., 2018

rappel.q: How many sides does square breathing have?

cards.titre: Square breathing
cards.texte: Inhale while counting to 4, hold your breath while counting to 4, exhale while counting to 4, wait 4. You draw a square with your breath and your body calms down.
cards.action: Try this today: do 3 breathing squares before going to sleep.

source.nom: Dimberg, Thunberg & Elmehed, Psychological Science, 2000

rappel.q: What does your face often do when you see a smile?

cards.titre: Smiles are contagious.
cards.texte: When someone smiles at you, your face tends to smile back, often without you even realizing it. Scientists have measured this using small sensors on the cheeks.
cards.action: Try this today: smile at 3 people and see if they smile back.

source.nom: Ekman & Friesen, JPSP, 1971

rappel.q: Who can recognize joy on a face?
choix: People from all over the world

cards.titre: All over the world, joy can be recognized on a face
cards.texte: A researcher showed photos of faces to people living far away, even in villages without television. Everyone recognized joy, fear, or anger. Emotions are a common language.
cards.action: Try it today: mime an emotion and have your family guess which one.

source.nom: Biddle & Asare, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2011 (revue)

rappel.q: What helps when you're grumpy?

cards.titre: Moving around helps when you're grumpy.
cards.texte: Running, dancing, or jumping is good for your mood. Studies on children show that physical activity helps them feel better and less tense.
cards.action: Try it today: dance for 3 minutes to your favorite song.
